stories.title: Apple falls 7%, Amazon jumps 12% after earnings — Wall Street is now picking AI 'winners and losers'
key_points: **Apple** beat on revenue and profit but fell **~7%** after warning of weaker guidance, citing **supply constraints**.
**Amazon** surged **~12%** even after raising its 2026 AI-infrastructure spending plan to about **$220 billion**, up from $200 billion.
The split: Amazon's cloud arm **AWS** grew fast enough to justify that spending; Apple's guidance suggested it isn't spending big on AI capacity at all.
Apple's iPhone and services revenue actually **topped estimates** — the stock fall was about the outlook, not the results themselves.
Investors who treated Apple as a **'safe' non-AI-spender** are now reconsidering, given Amazon and Microsoft's stronger numbers.
stories.background: Since 2023, the biggest US tech companies have been locked in a massive spending race on **AI infrastructure** — data centers, chips, and cloud capacity — betting that AI demand will keep growing fast enough to justify it. Investors have been split on whether this spending is smart growth or a bubble. Apple has mostly stayed out of that race, instead leaning on its iPhone/services business and using AI features built on partners' models rather than building its own giant data centers.
stories.what_happened: Apple and Amazon both reported quarterly earnings this week, and investors reacted in opposite directions. Apple's results **beat expectations** on revenue and per-share profit, but the company guided to **9–11% revenue growth** next quarter, below the roughly 12% analysts wanted, blaming **supply-chain constraints**. Its shares fell about **7%**. Amazon, by contrast, raised its planned 2026 capital spending to roughly **$220 billion** — up from a prior $200 billion estimate — mostly to keep building AI data-center capacity, and its stock still jumped about **12%**, because its cloud unit AWS showed strong enough growth to make that spending look justified rather than wasteful.
stories.why_it_matters: This is the market openly separating AI 'winners' from 'losers' for the first time this earnings season: heavy AI spending is now being rewarded when it comes with matching revenue growth, and punished when a company's growth story looks shaky regardless of the reason. It signals investors are getting pickier about the AI trade after two years of rewarding almost any AI-related spending increase.
stories.ripple_effects: Expect the same 'spend-and-grow vs. spend-without-growth' lens to be applied to Microsoft, Meta, and Google in the earnings that follow. Apple's stock weakness could revive questions about whether it's falling behind in AI capability. A sustained AWS growth story also strengthens Amazon's case that its enormous capex is paying off, which could pressure rivals to spend even more.
stories.why_now: This is Apple and Amazon's regular quarterly earnings report, but the size of the stock swings reflects how sensitive investors have become to any signal about whether AI spending is paying off.
stories.watch_next: Microsoft, Meta, and Google's upcoming earnings calls — watch whether their cloud/AI growth numbers justify their own capex increases the way AWS did for Amazon.

key_terms.definition: Money a company spends building long-term assets like data centers and chips, rather than day-to-day operating costs.
A company's own forecast for its future revenue or profit, given alongside its actual results.

stories.the_lesson: Markets don't just reward or punish spending in isolation — they reward spending that comes with visible proof it's generating growth, and punish spending (or a lack of it) that doesn't come with a growth story to match. The same dollar figure can be good news or bad news depending on what it's buying.
stories.market_link: Directly moves AAPL and AMZN, and is a read-through for MSFT, META, GOOGL ahead of their earnings; also a signal for AI-infrastructure suppliers (chipmakers, data-center operators).

stories.title: Nearly 50,000 migrants cross into Spain's Ceuta enclave in 24 hours; at least 18 die, Spain sends in the army
key_points: Spain's Interior Ministry says **almost 50,000 migrants** crossed from Morocco into Ceuta in a single 24-hour window — the **biggest surge since 2021**.
At least **18 people have died**, mostly by drowning or in a crush at the Tarajal breakwater, where many swam around the border fence.
Ceuta's population is only about **83,000**, so the influx briefly grew the city by roughly **50%** overnight.
Spain is deploying its **Armed Forces** to back up the Civil Guard, with PM **Pedro Sánchez** visiting Friday.
Local officials link the surge to a **Spanish Supreme Court ruling** that barred summarily returning migrants who arrive by sea without due process.
stories.background: Ceuta is a small **Spanish city on the North African coast**, bordering Morocco — one of only two land borders between the EU and Africa (the other being Melilla). Because it's Spanish (and EU) territory, it has long been a magnet for migrants trying to reach Europe, and periodic mass border-rush attempts have happened before, including a large one in 2021. Morocco normally polices its side of the border under an informal arrangement with Spain, so a surge this size suggests either a deliberate loosening of controls or a sudden breakdown of coordination between the two governments.
stories.what_happened: Beginning Thursday, July 30, thousands of people — the vast majority Moroccan nationals — rushed the Ceuta border, many wading and swimming around the breakwater fence where it meets the sea at Tarajal beach. Spain's Interior Ministry estimated **almost 50,000 crossings in 24 hours**, compared with only 1,500–2,000 over the previous ten days combined. At least **18 people died**, some by drowning, others in the crush of the crossing itself. Spain's government said Thursday evening it would send in the **Armed Forces** to help the Civil Guard restore order, and Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, alongside Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska, was set to visit Ceuta on Friday. Ceuta's local government has warned the city cannot absorb an influx of this scale.
stories.why_it_matters: This is the largest single-day migration event at a European border in years, and it lands directly on the EU's asylum and border-control system at a moment when migration is already one of the bloc's most politically explosive issues. How Spain and the EU respond — deportations, asylum processing, or a diplomatic reckoning with Morocco — will shape migration policy well beyond this one incident.
stories.ripple_effects: Expect a sharp domestic political fight in Spain over border security and asylum law, likely reviving pressure to overturn or narrow the Supreme Court ruling that limited summary returns. Morocco-Spain relations, already a delicate balance (Morocco polices the border in exchange for Spanish backing on Western Sahara), could come under strain if Madrid believes Rabat let the surge happen deliberately. The EU will likely face renewed pressure to fund border enforcement and migrant reception in southern member states.
stories.why_now: The trigger appears to be a recent Spanish Supreme Court ruling limiting summary returns of sea arrivals, which local officials say created an incentive to cross now rather than later — combined with what looks like a lapse in Moroccan border policing.
stories.watch_next: Watch for Spain's response to Morocco (diplomatic protest or quiet negotiation) and whether the EU offers emergency support to Ceuta in the coming days.

key_terms.definition: A piece of a country's territory that is geographically cut off from the main part of that country — Ceuta is Spanish land physically attached only to Morocco.
Immediately sending a migrant back across the border without a full asylum hearing; courts can require due process instead.

stories.the_lesson: Border crises like this are rarely just about the day of the crossing — they usually trace back to a specific policy or legal trigger (here, a court ruling) that changes the incentives for when people decide to move. Understanding the trigger matters more than the raw headline number.

stories.title: The rupee claws back to a near three-week high after the RBI sells $7 billion to defend it
key_points: The rupee strengthened to around **95.67 per dollar**, its best level in nearly **three weeks**.
It was the currency's **fourth straight session of gains**, its best run in four months.
The **Reserve Bank of India sold about $7 billion** in a single session earlier to stop an earlier slide.
A **pullback in oil prices** and the **dollar's biggest slide in three months** also helped the rupee.
The rupee had touched a **record low near 96.84** to the dollar earlier this year before this recovery.
stories.background: The rupee had been sliding toward record lows earlier this year, squeezed by elevated oil prices, US tariff moves, and rising US bond yields that pulled money out of emerging markets like India and toward the US dollar. A weak rupee makes everything India imports — from oil to electronics — more expensive, feeding inflation, and the RBI's playbook for defending the currency is to sell dollars from its foreign-exchange reserves to soak up demand for the greenback. It intervened aggressively before, at one point reportedly selling around $7 billion in a single day to defend the currency near its record low.
stories.what_happened: The rupee strengthened to around 95.67 per dollar, extending its gains for a fourth straight session to reach its strongest level in nearly three weeks, according to currency market reports. The move was driven by the US dollar's biggest slide in three months and a modest pullback in oil prices, combined with sustained, aggressive intervention by the **Reserve Bank of India**, which has continued selling dollars from its reserves to support the currency. The rupee is up about 0.9% for the week, on track for its best weekly showing in four months. This marks a notable reversal from earlier concern that the rupee was under renewed pressure as rising US bond yields squeezed the RBI's options.
stories.why_it_matters: A stronger rupee eases some of the inflation pressure from costlier imports, particularly oil, and gives the RBI more breathing room ahead of its Monetary Policy Committee meeting scheduled for early August. It's also a signal that central-bank intervention, while costly in reserves, can still move the currency meaningfully in the short term.
stories.ripple_effects: Cheaper imports and a steadier currency benefit companies that import raw materials or components, and reduce the near-term risk of imported inflation. But heavy, sustained RBI dollar-selling draws down India's foreign-exchange reserves, which are a buffer against future shocks — so the relief has a real cost attached to it.
stories.why_now: A weaker US dollar globally (its steepest slide in three months) combined with softer oil prices gave the RBI's ongoing intervention more room to actually move the rupee, after weeks of fighting a much stronger headwind.
stories.watch_next: Whether the rupee holds these gains into the RBI's Monetary Policy Committee meeting in early August, where the repo rate decision will be announced.

key_terms.definition: When a central bank buys or sells its own currency (using its foreign-currency reserves) to push the exchange rate in a desired direction.

stories.the_lesson: Currency moves are rarely about one country alone — a weaker dollar globally can lift the rupee just as much as anything India itself does, which is why central banks watch international rate and dollar trends as closely as domestic ones.
stories.market_link: A stronger rupee is broadly positive for import-heavy Indian sectors (oil marketing companies, electronics) and eases pressure on inflation-sensitive bonds; it's a mild negative for IT and export-driven services firms that earn in dollars.

thread.previously: The rupee was reported to be under renewed pressure as rising US bond yields squeezed the RBI's options for defending the currency.
thread.changed: The rupee has since reversed course, rising for a fourth straight session to a near three-week high, helped by a weaker dollar globally, softer oil prices, and the RBI selling roughly $7 billion to support it.

stories.title: Modi's Cabinet clears ₹5,070 crore scheme to float solar panels on India's reservoirs
key_points: The new **'PM Surya Sarovar Yojana'** targets **5,000 MW** of floating solar power with attached battery storage.
The government will pay developers **₹1 crore (about $120,000) per MW** in support once projects are commissioned.
Projects run from **FY2026-27 to FY2030-31**, with payouts continuing through FY2032-33.
The scheme is expected to **cut CO₂ emissions by 10 million tonnes a year** and create **16,000-17,000 jobs**.
It uses **reservoirs and industrial ponds** instead of land, sidestepping India's land-acquisition bottleneck for new solar.
stories.background: India has been racing to add renewable power capacity to meet both its climate targets and surging electricity demand, but large ground-mounted solar farms often get stuck in slow, contentious **land acquisition** — buying up or leasing the land needed to build them. Floating solar — panels mounted on rafts over reservoirs, canals or industrial ponds — sidesteps that problem entirely and has the added benefit of reducing water evaporation from the reservoir underneath. The scheme was cleared at the same Union Cabinet meeting on July 31 that also approved a large offshore oil-and-gas exploration push and an extension of the country's main farmer income-support scheme, underlining a broader push to lock in big-ticket infrastructure and welfare spending ahead of the 2026-27 fiscal year.
stories.what_happened: The Union Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, approved the 'Pradhan Mantri Surya Sarovar Yojana (PM-SSY)' on July 31, a scheme to build floating solar photovoltaic projects paired with **energy storage systems** on reservoirs and industrial ponds. The plan targets **5,000 MW of capacity**, with the government offering **central financial assistance of ₹1 crore per MW** to developers once projects are commissioned, plus additional support for feasibility studies. The total outlay is **₹5,070 crore**, with projects to be sanctioned between FY2026-27 and FY2030-31 and financial support disbursed through FY2032-33. The government projects the scheme will cut CO₂ emissions by roughly 10 million tonnes annually, generate 16,000-17,000 jobs, and boost domestic manufacturing of solar components in line with its 'Aatmanirbhar Bharat' (self-reliant India) push.
stories.why_it_matters: By building on water instead of land, the scheme removes one of the biggest practical obstacles to scaling up Indian solar power quickly. It also adds storage from the start, addressing solar's core weakness — that it only generates power when the sun is out.
stories.ripple_effects: Domestic solar-equipment makers and energy-storage suppliers stand to benefit from a new pipeline of demand, while states with large reservoirs (like those with big hydropower dams) gain a new use for that water infrastructure. If it scales as planned, it also reduces India's reliance on coal power and imported fuel over time, with knock-on benefits for the current account and air quality.
stories.why_now: The approval came in a single, large July 31 Cabinet meeting that also cleared other major infrastructure and welfare schemes, reflecting a government push to lock in multi-year spending commitments before the new fiscal year's budget cycle.
stories.watch_next: How quickly states identify reservoirs and industrial ponds and developers start bidding for the first tranche of projects.

key_terms.definition: Solar panels mounted on floating platforms on reservoirs or ponds instead of on land, which avoids land-acquisition costs and reduces water evaporation underneath.

stories.the_lesson: When land is the bottleneck for building new infrastructure, putting it on water (or otherwise reusing existing space) can unlock projects far faster than fighting through land-acquisition politics.
stories.market_link: Positive for listed Indian solar-module and energy-storage manufacturers and EPC (engineering, procurement, construction) firms likely to bid for these projects.

stories.title: India's August money rules kick in: a new nationwide KYC system and revised LPG prices
key_points: **CKYC 2.0** — a single, shared identity-verification record for banks, insurers and mutual funds — formally launches today, August 1.
It replaces repeated paperwork with **real-time, OTP-based verification** using just your mobile number or PAN.
State-run oil firms **IOCL, HPCL and BPCL** revise domestic and commercial LPG cylinder prices today, as they do on the 1st of every month.
The changes track **international crude and LPG benchmark prices** plus the rupee's exchange rate, so the new price varies by city.
They arrive alongside a wider bundle of 1st-of-the-month changes, including new **Tatkal train-ticket booking rules** and an ITR-filing penalty deadline.
stories.background: India has long required customers to submit the same identity documents separately to every bank, insurer, and mutual fund they deal with — a process called KYC ('Know Your Customer'), meant to prevent fraud and money laundering. A **Central KYC Registry (CKYC)**, run by an RBI/SEBI/IRDAI-backed body, already lets institutions share a customer's verified records, but the system has been clunky. LPG (cooking gas) cylinder prices, meanwhile, are reviewed and adjusted every month by India's state oil marketing companies based on global fuel costs — a routine but closely watched process because gas costs affect nearly every household budget.
stories.what_happened: From August 1, **CKYC 2.0** goes live as the formally upgraded version of India's shared KYC framework, described as a move toward a 'One KYC' system. It uses real-time APIs and secure OTP-based consent so that once a customer's identity is verified with one institution, a bank, insurer, or fund house can pull the same verified record instantly using just a mobile number or PAN card — instead of asking the customer to resubmit documents each time. On the same day, IOCL, HPCL and BPCL announced their monthly revision of **domestic and commercial LPG cylinder prices** for brands like Indane, Bharat Gas and HP Gas; because the change depends on international crude and LPG benchmark prices and the rupee's exchange rate, actual new prices differ by city. The changes land alongside several other rules that reset on the 1st of the month, including revised Tatkal railway ticket booking procedures and ITR (income tax return) late-filing penalty deadlines for salaried employees.
stories.why_it_matters: CKYC 2.0 is meant to cut the friction and paperwork that slows down opening a bank account, buying insurance, or investing in a mutual fund in India — a small change with a large reach given how many first-time users enter India's formal financial system each year. The LPG price revision directly affects household budgets nationwide, since cooking gas is a near-universal monthly expense.
stories.ripple_effects: Faster KYC could speed up account-opening and onboarding for banks, insurers, and fintech apps, and may nudge more first-time users into formal financial products. LPG price moves feed into India's retail inflation basket, so a price rise (or cut) shows up, in a small way, in the next Consumer Price Index reading the RBI watches when setting interest rates.
stories.why_now: Both changes are calendar-driven: LPG prices reset on the 1st of every month by design, and CKYC 2.0's formal rollout date was set by regulators for August 1.
stories.watch_next: Watch whether banks and insurers report faster onboarding times in the weeks after CKYC 2.0 goes live, and check your city's specific new LPG cylinder price, since it isn't uniform nationwide.

key_terms.definition: The identity-verification process banks and other financial firms are legally required to do before opening an account for someone.
A shared, government-backed database that stores a customer's verified KYC record so multiple financial institutions can reuse it instead of each collecting documents separately.

stories.the_lesson: A lot of meaningful economic change happens through unglamorous plumbing fixes like shared identity databases, not just headline policy announcements — friction removed from everyday transactions compounds across millions of people.

stories.title: The Supreme Court ends Jammu & Kashmir CM Omar Abdullah's 17-year divorce battle, closing the case by mutual settlement
key_points: The Supreme Court granted a **mutual-consent divorce** to Jammu & Kashmir Chief Minister **Omar Abdullah** and his estranged wife **Payal Abdullah**.
The couple married in **1994** and had been **living separately since 2009** — a legal fight that ran roughly **17 years**.
A family court had earlier **rejected** Abdullah's divorce petition, a ruling upheld by a Delhi High Court bench in **2023**.
The case was resolved after the Supreme Court referred it to **mediation**, where both sides reached a full settlement.
Senior advocate **Kapil Sibal** represented Abdullah; the bench included Justices **PS Narasimha** and **Alok Aradhe**.
stories.background: Omar Abdullah is the sitting Chief Minister of Jammu and Kashmir and a senior leader of the National Conference party, and the son of former Jammu and Kashmir Chief Minister Farooq Abdullah — one of the most prominent political families in the region. He married Payal Abdullah, who is of British-Sikh descent, in 1994, and the couple has been estranged and living separately since 2009, though the marriage was never formally dissolved for years despite Abdullah seeking it. A family court rejected his divorce petition in 2016 for failing to prove grounds like cruelty or desertion, and a Delhi High Court bench upheld that rejection in December 2023, pushing the matter to the Supreme Court.
stories.what_happened: The Supreme Court, in a bench of Justices **PS Narasimha and Alok Aradhe**, granted a mutual-consent divorce to Omar Abdullah and Payal Abdullah, closing a legal battle that had run since he first sought dissolution of the marriage. The two had married on **September 1, 1994**, and lived separately since **2009**. After lower courts repeatedly rejected Abdullah's petition — a family court in 2016 and a Delhi High Court division bench in December 2023 — the Supreme Court referred the matter to its **Mediation Centre**, where the two sides worked out a complete settlement. Senior advocate **Kapil Sibal**, appearing for Abdullah, told the court the parties had resolved all outstanding issues and agreed to withdraw related proceedings, after which the bench disposed of the case.
stories.why_it_matters: The case is a high-profile example of India's Supreme Court increasingly using its mediation centre to resolve long-pending matrimonial disputes rather than letting them run through years of adversarial litigation, especially once both parties want out. It also closes a long personal chapter for one of India's most prominent state-level political leaders as he continues to govern Jammu & Kashmir.
stories.ripple_effects: The resolution removes a long-running personal legal matter from Abdullah's public profile as he continues as Jammu & Kashmir's Chief Minister. It may also be cited by family-law practitioners as a model case for using court-referred mediation to settle protracted matrimonial disputes.
stories.why_now: The case reached this point now because the Supreme Court's mediation process, initiated after years of lower-court rejections, finally produced an agreement both parties were willing to sign off on.
stories.watch_next: No further legal proceedings are expected, as the Supreme Court has disposed of the matter entirely.

key_terms.definition: A divorce granted when both spouses agree to end the marriage and its terms, which Indian courts can finalize faster than a contested divorce.

stories.the_lesson: Even a legal case that drags on for nearly two decades can resolve quickly once both sides genuinely want a settlement — courts increasingly use structured mediation to get there instead of forcing years of adversarial hearings.

stories.title: India's Cabinet approves a ₹36,441 crore overhaul of the Khelo India sports scheme, betting big after its best-ever Commonwealth Games showing
key_points: The Union Cabinet approved a revamped **Khelo India Scheme** with a combined outlay of **₹36,441 crore** for **2026-27 to 2030-31**.
It replaces an earlier five-year plan that had a smaller **₹29,000 crore** outlay.
New initiatives include **Khelo India Feeder Schools** and **Utkrishta Vidyalayas**, building a pipeline from school sport to the Olympic podium.
The eligible athlete pool expands **nearly ten-fold** through a new 'Emerging Khelo India Athletes' category.
The approval lands **during the Commonwealth Games**, where India's team is having its best-ever medal haul.
stories.background: Khelo India is the Indian government's flagship scheme to develop grassroots sporting talent, built to create a structured pipeline of athletes from school competitions up through elite training centers, in response to India's historically modest medal counts at global multi-sport events relative to its population. Earlier iterations funded state-level competitions, sports infrastructure, and stipends for promising young athletes, but coaches and administrators have long argued the funding and athlete-identification numbers were too small to match India's ambitions. The **Union Cabinet**, chaired by Prime Minister **Narendra Modi**, has periodically extended and expanded the scheme, this time increasing its outlay again just as India's team delivers a record medal haul at the ongoing 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.
stories.what_happened: The Union Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, approved an expanded Khelo India Scheme along with enhanced Assistance to National Sports Federations (ANSFs), with a combined outlay of **₹36,441 crore** running from **2026-27 through 2030-31** — up from an earlier five-year allocation of roughly ₹29,000 crore. Information and Broadcasting Minister **Ashwini Vaishnaw** announced the decision, which introduces new programs including **Khelo India Feeder Schools** and **Utkrishta Vidyalayas** (excellence-focused schools) meant to identify talented young athletes earlier and track them through a structured development pipeline. The scheme also creates an **'Emerging Khelo India Athletes'** category that expands the pool of athletes eligible for state support by roughly **ten times** its previous size. The decision comes as India's contingent has its best-ever Commonwealth Games campaign in Glasgow, with a record number of boxing finalists and medals across multiple sports.
stories.why_it_matters: This is a direct government bet that more sustained, earlier-stage funding will translate into more Olympic and Commonwealth-level medals — closing a long-standing gap between India's population size and its sporting success. The roughly 25% funding increase signals sports policy is being treated as a multi-year infrastructure investment, not just event-by-event spending.
stories.ripple_effects: State sports academies, coaches and equipment suppliers should see a meaningful funding boost over the next five years. A wider athlete pool under the new 'Emerging' category means more young athletes outside major cities could get access to structured training and stipends, potentially reshaping where India's next generation of Olympians comes from. National Sports Federations, which govern individual sports, also get enhanced funding, easing long-running complaints about inadequate support for non-cricket sports.
stories.why_now: The approval comes as India's Commonwealth Games team delivers its best-ever medal performance, giving the government a high-visibility moment to expand sports funding while public attention and athlete momentum are both high.
stories.watch_next: How quickly the Khelo India Feeder Schools and Utkrishta Vidyalayas are rolled out, and whether the funding shows up in India's medal count at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.

key_terms.definition: India's top decision-making body of senior ministers, chaired by the Prime Minister, which approves major government schemes and policies.

stories.the_lesson: Sustained sporting success rarely comes from one big push before a major event — it comes from years of earlier, structural investment in identifying and training athletes, which is why policy shifts like this are judged years later, not in the next Games cycle.

stories.title: Modi's Cabinet extends India's biggest farmer cash-support scheme through 2031, at a cost of ₹3.15 lakh crore
key_points: The Union Cabinet approved continuing **PM-KISAN** from **2026-27 to 2030-31**, at a cost of **₹3.15 lakh crore** (roughly $38 billion).
Under the scheme, eligible farmers get **₹2,000 three times a year** (₹6,000/year), paid directly into their bank accounts.
Over **₹4.47 lakh crore** has been paid out across **23 installments** since the scheme launched in 2019.
The government says **85% of farmers** report borrowing less because of the guaranteed income support.
stories.background: **PM-KISAN** (Pradhan Mantri Kisan Samman Nidhi) is a flagship Modi government scheme launched in 2019 that gives small and marginal farmers direct cash payments using **Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT)** — money sent straight to bank accounts rather than through subsidized inputs or middlemen. It is one of the largest direct cash-transfer programs to farmers anywhere in the world. The extension comes as rural income and farm distress remain a persistent political and economic issue in India.
stories.what_happened: The Union Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, approved continuing PM-KISAN for a further five years, from **2026-27 to 2030-31**, with a total financial outlay of **₹3.15 lakh crore**. The scheme pays ₹2,000 three times a year directly into farmers' bank accounts via DBT. Officials said more than **₹4.47 lakh crore** has already been transferred across 23 installments since the scheme began, and that internal studies show **85% of farmers** have cut back on borrowing because of the guaranteed payments. The Cabinet said continuing the scheme would help farmers invest in agriculture, improve productivity, reduce farming risk, and strengthen the rural economy.
stories.why_it_matters: PM-KISAN reaches tens of millions of farmers and is a central plank of the government's rural economic strategy. Committing to fund it for five more years signals continued fiscal support for farm incomes at a time when rural distress and farmer demands — including a legal guarantee for minimum crop prices — remain politically live issues.
stories.ripple_effects: Sustained direct payments can support rural consumption — more cash in farmers' hands often lifts demand for consumer goods, two-wheelers and farm equipment in rural India. The ₹3.15 lakh crore commitment is also a major multi-year claim on the federal budget, and the move is likely to be read as a political signal to India's large farming electorate.
stories.why_now: The scheme's current funding cycle was due to lapse, so the Cabinet needed to approve a renewal before the new fiscal year (2026-27) begins.
stories.watch_next: Whether the government pairs this with movement on farmers' other long-standing demands, such as a legal guarantee for MSP (minimum support price).

key_terms.definition: A system where government welfare payments go straight into a recipient's bank account electronically, instead of through cash or middlemen — meant to cut leakage and corruption.

stories.the_lesson: Direct cash transfers, done at national scale, can measurably change how households borrow and spend — but they're also a recurring fiscal commitment, not a one-time expense, so extending one is itself a major budget decision.
stories.market_link: Rural-focused consumer goods, two-wheeler and tractor makers can see a modest sentiment boost from continued farm income-support spending.

stories.title: Neeraj Chopra wins silver as Sri Lanka's Rumesh Pathirage takes Commonwealth Games javelin gold

thread.previously: Neeraj Chopra scraped through qualifying into the men's javelin final at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, setting up a final-night showdown with defending champion Arshad Nadeem of Pakistan.
thread.changed: In the final, Chopra threw 85.83m to win silver, finishing behind Sri Lanka's Rumesh Tharanga Pathirage, who won gold with 89.75m. India's Yash Vir Singh took bronze with a personal-best 85.41m on his Games debut. Nadeem, the defending champion, was eliminated after three rounds and finished ninth at 77.41m.

key_points: Neeraj Chopra won **silver** with a throw of **85.83m** — his **second Commonwealth Games medal** after gold at Gold Coast 2018.
Sri Lanka's **Rumesh Tharanga Pathirage** won gold with **89.75m**, upsetting the pre-final favourites.
India's **Yash Vir Singh** claimed bronze with a personal-best **85.41m** on his Commonwealth Games debut — a **double podium** for India.
Defending champion **Arshad Nadeem** of Pakistan was eliminated after three rounds, finishing **ninth** at 77.41m.
stories.background: Neeraj Chopra is India's biggest track-and-field star and the country's **Olympic javelin gold medalist** from Tokyo 2020, which made him a national icon in a sport India had rarely excelled at internationally. His rivalry with Pakistan's **Arshad Nadeem** — the reigning Olympic silver medalist and defending Commonwealth Games champion — has become one of athletics' most closely watched storylines, partly because of the two countries' tense relationship outside sport. Chopra had a shaky qualifying round, barely making Friday's final.
stories.what_happened: In the men's javelin final at **Scotstoun Stadium in Glasgow**, Neeraj Chopra threw **85.83m** to win the silver medal, his second Commonwealth Games medal after winning gold at Gold Coast in 2018. Sri Lanka's **Rumesh Tharanga Pathirage** produced the throw of the competition, **89.75m**, to take gold and deny both India and Pakistan's stars. India's **Yash Vir Singh**, on his Commonwealth Games debut, threw a personal-best **85.41m** to claim bronze, giving India a double podium in the event. Pakistan's **Arshad Nadeem**, the defending champion, struggled badly and was eliminated after three rounds, finishing ninth with a best of just 77.41m — a shock exit for the reigning Olympic silver medalist.
stories.why_it_matters: Chopra extends his medal streak at a marquee global event and India lands a rare double podium in one of its highest-profile athletics events. Nadeem's shock elimination reshapes the competitive picture in men's javelin heading into future majors.
stories.ripple_effects: This boosts India's overall medal tally and morale at the Games, and raises Yash Vir Singh's profile as a rising javelin talent to watch. It also puts scrutiny on Pakistan's athletics preparation after their biggest star had an off day on the sport's biggest stage.
stories.why_now: The men's javelin final was the marquee session of Commonwealth Games athletics on the day, closing out one of the meet's most anticipated events.
stories.watch_next: Whether Chopra addresses his qualifying struggles and current form, and how Nadeem responds after an uncharacteristic off day.

key_terms.definition: The best result an athlete has ever recorded in an event — beating your PB means outperforming every previous attempt of your own career.

stories.the_lesson: Making the final is only half the job — delivering under pressure is the other half. Chopra's shaky qualifying didn't stop him medaling, while the defending champion's bad day cost him a place on the podium entirely.
