stories.title: Lewis Hamilton shuts down the theory that 2026's new rules just happen to suit his driving style
key_points: Hamilton says the **2026 regulations** aren't inherently 'more rewarding' for his style, pushing back on a common fan/media theory.
He's had his **best season with Ferrari** since joining — **169 points**, five podiums in six races, and his **first win for the team**, at Barcelona.
2025, his first Ferrari season, was reportedly the **worst of his career** — no podiums at all.
The turnaround has fueled speculation the new car rules simply favor how Hamilton naturally drives, which he's now directly disputed.
The comments come heading into F1's **summer break**, a natural moment for reflection on the season so far.
stories.background: Formula 1 introduced a **major regulation overhaul for the 2026 season** — new car designs, power units and rules — which resets the competitive order and changes how much a driver's individual style matters versus the car itself. Lewis Hamilton, a seven-time world champion, moved to **Ferrari** for 2025 and endured what's been called the worst season of his career, failing to reach a single podium. His marked improvement in 2026 has led some to argue the new rules simply favor his particular driving technique, rather than reflecting genuine gains from him or the team.
stories.what_happened: Speaking ahead of F1's summer break, Lewis Hamilton **rejected the idea** that the 2026 regulation changes are simply more suited to his driving style than to other drivers'. He said he hasn't had to change his approach more than usual to adapt to the new cars. The comments come after a season in which Hamilton has scored **169 points** with **five podiums in six races**, including his **first Grand Prix win for Ferrari**, in Barcelona — a sharp contrast to a winless, podium-less 2025.
stories.why_it_matters: How much credit goes to the driver versus the car is a recurring, high-stakes argument in F1 that shapes driver reputations, contract negotiations, and team strategy. Hamilton publicly disputing the 'rules favor me' narrative is him defending his own performance as genuine skill and adaptation, not a lucky rule change.
stories.ripple_effects: The debate affects how rivals, teams and sponsors value Hamilton heading into future contract talks, and feeds the broader conversation about whether F1's 2026 rules have been well-designed or are producing unpredictable, driver-dependent results.
stories.why_now: The comments come as F1 heads into its summer break, a natural checkpoint for reviewing the season, and after growing media speculation tied to Hamilton's turnaround since his difficult 2025.
stories.watch_next: Whether Hamilton can maintain podium form in the second half of the season, when the summer break ends.
stories.the_lesson: When a driver or team's fortunes suddenly change after a rule shift, it's tempting to credit the rules alone — but genuine performance turnarounds usually involve real adaptation work that's easy to underrate from the outside.

stories.title: F1 sets a September deadline to decide if its season finale moves out of the Middle East
key_points: F1 has set a **mid-September deadline** to decide the fate of the season-ending **Qatar and Abu Dhabi** Grands Prix
If those races can't safely go ahead, F1 will end the 2026 season with a **European race instead**
**Imola**, dropped from this year's calendar, is the leading candidate to host a replacement finale
The uncertainty follows the earlier cancellation of the **Bahrain and Saudi Arabian** Grands Prix this season over the **US-Iran conflict**
Both Qatar and Abu Dhabi remain on the calendar and are **already sold out**
stories.background: F1's calendar has leaned increasingly on Middle East races in recent years — Bahrain, Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Abu Dhabi have all hosted rounds, drawn by state investment and glamorous season-finale slots. That bet has run into trouble in 2026: escalating regional tension tied to the **US-Iran conflict** already forced F1 to scrap the Bahrain and Saudi Arabian rounds earlier this season. Qatar and Abu Dhabi, scheduled to close out the year, are now the ones in question, and F1 has been monitoring the security situation rather than committing to a call either way.
stories.what_happened: Formula 1 has told teams it will make a final decision on the Qatar and Abu Dhabi Grands Prix by **mid-September**, based on how the regional security situation develops. If the races are judged unsafe to hold, F1 has said it will shift its season finale to **Europe** rather than find another venue further afield — partly because a like-for-like replacement is hard to source on short notice, and partly to avoid clashing with the NFL season in the US, which rules out adding an extra American round. **Imola**, the Italian circuit that lost its slot on the 2026 calendar, has emerged as the leading candidate to host a replacement European finale despite it being an unusual time of year, weather-wise, for the track.
stories.why_it_matters: F1 has spent years building its business model around lucrative, spectacle-heavy Middle East races — this is the clearest sign yet that geopolitical instability can force the sport to unwind that bet on short notice, with real financial and logistical consequences for teams, broadcasters and host cities.
stories.ripple_effects: Teams have to plan car development and logistics around two very different possible calendars; Qatar and Abu Dhabi face reputational and financial hits if their races are pulled after selling out tickets; and a shift to Imola would be a boost for European fans even as it underscores how fragile the current calendar's Middle East expansion has become.
stories.why_now: The decision window is opening now because F1 needs lead time to finalize logistics either way, and the regional security picture tied to the US-Iran conflict remains unresolved enough that F1 isn't ready to commit yet.
stories.watch_next: Watch for F1's mid-September announcement — that's the hard deadline by which the sport says it will confirm whether the season ends in the Middle East or in Europe.
stories.the_lesson: Sports calendars built around geopolitically sensitive regions carry a hidden fragility — the more a business depends on stability it doesn't control, the more exposed it is when that stability breaks.

stories.title: Red Bull offers Max Verstappen $80 million a year to stay through 2029 — and to give up his escape hatch
key_points: Red Bull has offered Verstappen roughly **$80 million a year** to extend through **2029**, up from his current deal running to 2028
The catch: the new contract would **remove his exit clause**, the performance trigger that currently lets him leave
That clause lets Verstappen quit Red Bull if he's **outside the top two** in the standings at the summer break — he's currently **P6**
Verstappen has had the offer for **several weeks** and hasn't responded; he has until **mid-October** to decide
Both **Mercedes and McLaren** are reportedly watching the situation closely
stories.background: Max Verstappen has won **four consecutive F1 drivers' championships** with Red Bull, but the team's competitiveness has dipped in 2026 relative to McLaren and others, feeding a season-long storyline about whether the four-time champion might leave. His current contract, signed during Red Bull's dominant years, contains an unusual **performance-based exit clause**: if he's not running P1 or P2 in the championship by the summer break, he can walk. That clause exists precisely because Red Bull wanted to reassure Verstappen it would keep the car competitive — and now that the car isn't, the clause has become live leverage.
stories.what_happened: Red Bull has put a new contract offer in front of Verstappen's management: roughly **$80 million per year**, extending his stay through the end of **2029** (a season beyond his current 2028 deal), with a pay rise attached. The trade-off is that the new deal would **strip out the exit clause** entirely — meaning if he signs, Verstappen gives up his current right to leave based on where the team sits in the standings. He's currently **sixth** in the drivers' championship, which under his existing contract already qualifies him to trigger an exit if he wanted to. Verstappen's camp has reportedly held the offer for weeks without a formal response, and he says he's focused on getting the car faster rather than being distracted by contract talk. He has until **mid-October** to make a call.
stories.why_it_matters: This is the single biggest storyline in F1's driver market: a four-time champion, sitting on leverage to leave a struggling team, being offered a lot of money to give that leverage up voluntarily. Whichever way Verstappen goes reshapes the 2027 driver market — a Verstappen exit would open the sport's most coveted seat and trigger a chain reaction across multiple teams.
stories.ripple_effects: If Verstappen stays, Red Bull locks in stability and starts a car-development push to justify the faith he's shown; if he leaves, expect a scramble at Mercedes or McLaren to fit him in, likely displacing another driver, and Red Bull would need to find a replacement capable of anchoring the team. Sponsors, F1 broadcasters and betting markets are all watching this play out given how much of F1's audience is built around Verstappen's dominance.
stories.why_now: The clock is genuinely ticking — Verstappen's exit-clause window is open right now because he's below the top-two threshold, and Red Bull wants a decision before the driver market's other dominoes (Alonso, and the remaining out-of-contract half of the grid) fall into place.
stories.watch_next: Watch for any signal from Verstappen's camp before mid-October — a signed extension, a public commitment to a rival, or continued silence that lets speculation keep building.

key_terms.definition: A contract term letting a driver leave a team early if a specific condition — often a performance threshold — isn't met.

stories.the_lesson: Contracts encode leverage, not just salary — a clause tied to performance only matters when performance actually dips, and that's exactly when it becomes the most contested clause in the document.

stories.title: Carlos Sainz's Audi hopes take a hit as Gabriel Bortoleto declares he's staying 'for many years'
key_points: Audi-bound driver **Gabriel Bortoleto** says he is signed to the manufacturer for **'many years'**, undercutting rumours Carlos Sainz could take his seat.
**Carlos Sainz's Williams contract** runs only through the end of this season, and he had been linked to Red Bull, Aston Martin, and Audi for 2027.
Audi is currently transitioning the **Sauber team** into a full factory effort, with Bortoleto and Nico Hulkenberg originally thought to be signed only through 2026.
Sainz has reportedly **asked to be left out of driver-market speculation** ahead of a summer decision on his own future.
Audi has separately signalled interest in **other drivers**, adding to uncertainty over exactly who partners Bortoleto long-term.
stories.background: **Audi** is entering Formula 1 as a full factory manufacturer team from 2026 by taking over the existing **Sauber** team's entry — a common way new manufacturers join F1 without building a team from zero. It retained **Nico Hulkenberg and Gabriel Bortoleto**, Sauber's 2025 drivers, initially on deals many assumed ran only through this transition year. **Carlos Sainz**, a race-winning veteran now at Williams, is out of contract at the end of the season and had been widely tipped as a candidate for a big-name manufacturer seat like Audi's for 2027, especially given his experience and lack of a current race win at Williams.
stories.what_happened: **Gabriel Bortoleto said he is contracted to Audi for 'many years,'** a stronger commitment than previously assumed, which works against reports that **Carlos Sainz** could be lined up to replace him at the manufacturer for 2027. Bortoleto and teammate Nico Hulkenberg had signed two-year deals ahead of the 2025 season specifically to help oversee Sauber's transition into the full Audi factory team, but Bortoleto's comments suggest his tenure is meant to extend well beyond that. This leaves Sainz's situation more uncertain: his Williams contract runs out at the end of this season, and while he has been linked with Red Bull, Aston Martin and Audi, he has reportedly asked to stay out of driver-market speculation while he weighs his options over the summer break.
stories.why_it_matters: The 2027 driver market is one of the most closely watched in years because several top seats — including Audi's — are in flux, and where established race-winners like Sainz land shapes the competitive order for years. Bortoleto locking down his Audi seat removes one of the most talked-about options for Sainz.
stories.ripple_effects: If Audi's seats are effectively locked in, Sainz's remaining options narrow to Red Bull or Aston Martin, intensifying competition for those seats among other drivers too. It also affects Williams, which now has more time to plan Sainz's replacement rather than fighting to keep him.
stories.why_now: Bortoleto's comments came out during the mid-season driver market 'silly season' chatter, directly countering swirling reports linking Sainz to his seat, which is why the story is trending now.
stories.watch_next: Watch for Carlos Sainz's own announcement on his 2027 plans, expected after the summer break, and any confirmation from Red Bull or Aston Martin about his candidacy.

key_terms.definition: The informal F1 term for the period each year when driver contracts, transfers and rumors dominate the news before the next season's lineups are finalized.

stories.the_lesson: In competitive team sports, a talented incumbent publicly reaffirming their commitment can shut down a transfer rumor faster than any official statement from the team — words from the player often move the market as much as contracts do.

stories.title: Cadillac's F1 team allegedly tells UK staff: move to America or lose your job
key_points: Cadillac's Formula 1 team is reportedly **relocating operations to the US**, its home market, as it settles into its debut season.
UK-based staff have allegedly been told they must **relocate to America or be let go**.
The team, fielding **Valtteri Bottas and Sergio 'Checo' Perez**, is competing in its first-ever F1 season in 2026.
Cadillac's on-track results have been rough so far, with both cars starting recent races **near the back of the grid**.
The relocation report adds workforce uncertainty on top of the team's on-track struggles in its debut year.
stories.background: **Cadillac**, the American luxury brand owned by General Motors, joined Formula 1 as an entirely new team for the 2026 season — the first new constructor entry in years, following through on a long approval process with F1's governing bodies. It signed two experienced drivers, 10-time race winner Valtteri Bottas and six-time race winner Sergio Perez, to lead the new outfit. New F1 teams typically build their initial engineering base wherever they can hire experienced staff fastest — often the UK, home to most of F1's specialist supply chain — even if the team's brand and ownership are American.
stories.what_happened: Reports emerged that **Cadillac's Formula 1 team has told UK-based staff they must relocate to the United States or lose their jobs**, as the team works to consolidate operations closer to its American ownership and market. This comes as the team, in its **debut 2026 F1 season** with drivers Valtteri Bottas and Sergio Perez, has struggled on track — both cars have qualified and finished races near the back of the field at recent Grands Prix, including Hungary and Belgium. The relocation push suggests Cadillac wants a more US-centered engineering and operations base for the long term, even though much of its early hiring, like most new F1 teams, likely drew on the UK's deep pool of Formula 1 engineering talent.
stories.why_it_matters: How a brand-new F1 team structures itself in year one often determines whether it becomes a stable, competitive constructor or struggles for years — and workforce upheaval this early is a red flag for stability. It's also notable as the first American-owned works team in decades trying to build a US-based F1 operation instead of following the traditional UK-based model.
stories.ripple_effects: Losing UK-based staff who won't relocate could set back Cadillac's technical development at a critical early stage, potentially prolonging its back-of-the-grid form. It could also make it harder to attract experienced F1 engineers in the future if the team gets a reputation for instability.
stories.why_now: The story surfaces now as Cadillac's difficult debut season results collide with reports of this internal relocation ultimatum, drawing fresh scrutiny of the team's operational plans.
stories.watch_next: Watch for an official Cadillac F1 statement confirming or denying the relocation ultimatum, and any staff departures reported in the coming weeks.
stories.the_lesson: Building a competitive Formula 1 team takes years of stable technical continuity — any new team that disrupts its own workforce early, even for strategic reasons, risks losing the institutional knowledge that competitive teams depend on.

stories.title: Red Bull poaches Mercedes' junior-talent scout Gwen Lagrue to run its own young-driver program
key_points: Red Bull has signed **Gwen Lagrue**, Mercedes' junior-driver talent scout, to lead its own young-driver program from **2027**.
Lagrue built much of Mercedes' current junior pipeline, which has already produced F1 race winners.
Red Bull called its junior program **'a cornerstone of its success'** in announcing the hire.
The move is one of the most significant **personnel poaches between rival junior programs** in recent memory.
It comes as Red Bull's own driver lineup, including Max Verstappen's future, remains **unresolved for 2027**.
stories.background: F1 teams run 'junior' or 'academy' programs that scout, fund, and develop young karting and junior-formula drivers, betting that a few of them will eventually reach Formula 1. Mercedes' junior program, under Lagrue's guidance, has been widely credited with helping develop drivers who went on to strong Mercedes F1 seats, making the scouting and development pipeline itself a valuable, competitive asset — not just the drivers it produces. Red Bull has historically run one of the most aggressive and well-resourced junior programs on the grid, previously overseen for years by the late Helmut Marko.
stories.what_happened: Red Bull confirmed that **Gwen Lagrue**, who has led Mercedes' junior driver talent-scouting efforts, has agreed to join Red Bull starting in **2027** to lead its own young-driver program. Red Bull framed the hire as reinforcing the importance it places on developing future F1 talent, calling the junior programme 'a cornerstone of Red Bull's success.' The move effectively transfers a key piece of Mercedes' driver-development expertise to one of its biggest championship rivals.
stories.why_it_matters: Junior-driver pipelines are a long-term competitive advantage in F1 — losing the person who built yours to a direct rival is a real strategic setback that plays out over years, not just one season.
stories.ripple_effects: Mercedes will need to rebuild its scouting leadership, potentially slowing its junior pipeline just as Red Bull's gets a boost, which could shift which young drivers each team locks in over the next few seasons.
stories.why_now: The announcement lands amid a broader wave of driver-market news this week, as teams across the grid lock in personnel and driver plans ahead of the 2027 rule changes.
stories.watch_next: Watch which junior drivers Lagrue brings with her or immediately targets once she starts at Red Bull in 2027.

key_terms.definition: A team-run scheme that scouts, funds and develops young drivers through karting and junior racing categories, aiming to produce future F1 talent.

stories.the_lesson: In talent-driven industries, poaching the person who built a rival's pipeline can be more valuable than poaching any single product of that pipeline — the process itself is the asset.

stories.title: F1 rules out a second Las Vegas race for 2026, blaming Brexit paperwork and an NFL scheduling clash
key_points: F1 boss Stefano Domenicali confirmed a proposed **second Las Vegas race** for 2026 will not happen.
The idea was for a double-header weekend around **November 21**, which would have clashed with **NFL Weeks 10 and 11**.
Post-Brexit **UK customs paperwork** for F1's nine British-based teams added a major logistical hurdle to a quick second US race.
Domenicali said the alternative is to keep the season finale within the **same European logistics framework** F1 already uses.
F1 says it will finalize its **2027 calendar and Middle East race plans by September**.
stories.background: Formula 1 already holds one Las Vegas Grand Prix on its calendar, added in 2023 as a marquee US event on the Strip. With ongoing uncertainty over whether the sport's usual season-ending races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi can go ahead given the Middle East conflict, F1 had explored adding a second US race, potentially in Las Vegas, as a contingency. Most F1 teams are based in the UK, and since Brexit, moving cars, equipment, and freight in and out of the UK for races requires additional customs documentation that didn't exist before — a logistical cost that barely registered before 2020 but now shapes how quickly F1 can add or move race weekends.
stories.what_happened: F1 CEO Stefano Domenicali explained that a plan to hold a second Las Vegas race in 2026, as part of a possible double-header around **November 21**, has been scrapped. The date would have directly clashed with **NFL Weeks 10 and 11**, competing for the same fanbase and broadcast attention in the US market. Compounding the problem, adding an extra US race on short notice would have required F1's nine UK-based teams to complete an additional round of Brexit-related customs paperwork to move freight in and out of Britain — a bureaucratic hurdle Domenicali said made a quick second Vegas race impractical. Instead, F1 says if its usual season-ending Middle East races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi can't go ahead, it will fall back to holding the finale within Europe, inside its existing logistics setup, rather than adding a new US date. F1 says it expects to finalize both this year's contingency plan and its full 2027 calendar by September.
stories.why_it_matters: It shows how much post-Brexit logistics now constrain F1's ability to react quickly to a crisis, even when there's commercial appetite (a second marquee US race) to do so.
stories.ripple_effects: Teams and broadcasters lose out on a potentially lucrative second US race weekend this year, while European venues become the default fallback option for any late-season disruption, likely benefiting circuits like Imola that have hosted F1 before.
stories.why_now: This follows this week's broader F1 news that a Middle East-conflict-driven Europe fallback is being planned for the 2026 finale, prompting fans to ask why a second US race wasn't the answer instead.
stories.watch_next: Watch for F1's September announcement confirming both the 2026 finale venue and the full 2027 calendar.

key_terms.definition: The additional customs declarations UK-based teams must now file to move freight and equipment in and out of Britain for races, a requirement that didn't exist before the UK left the EU.

stories.the_lesson: Big commercial ideas can be blocked not by demand or money, but by logistics and bureaucracy — real-world constraints like customs rules and scheduling clashes often decide what's actually possible faster than strategy does.

stories.title: Aston Martin's F1 paddock mourns tyre technician Mick 'Biscuit' Fern, a 35-year veteran
key_points: Aston Martin tyre technician **Mick Fern**, known throughout the paddock as **'Biscuit'**, has died.
He spent **35 years in the F1 paddock**, joining the team in **1999** when it raced as Jordan.
The team announced his passing on Instagram, saying he died **'peacefully'**.
Driver **Lance Stroll** led tributes, calling him **'one of a kind'** after 7 years working together.
Teams across the grid marked his absence at the Hungarian Grand Prix with signs and shows of support.
stories.background: Behind every F1 driver is a large team of mechanics and technicians who rarely get public recognition but are essential to a car actually running — tyre technicians like Fern manage the preparation and fitting of tyres, one of the most safety-critical jobs in the pit lane. Fern's F1 career stretched back to 1999 with the Jordan team, a now-defunct outfit whose successor entities eventually became today's Aston Martin — meaning he'd been part of the same team's lineage for over a quarter-century of F1's modern era.
stories.what_happened: Aston Martin announced on Wednesday that Mick Fern, affectionately nicknamed 'Biscuit' and known across the paddock over his 35-year F1 career, had passed away. The team's statement said 'the thoughts of the entire team and F1 community are with the family and friends of our teammate.' Fern had most recently worked as one of Aston Martin's tyre technicians. His absence was visibly marked at the Hungarian Grand Prix, with the team placing a sign reading 'Biscuit. Thinking of you' outside its garage and on the grid, and figures from across the paddock gathering for a show of support. Driver Lance Stroll, who worked with Fern for seven years, said: 'You always made me laugh in the back of the garage, and you truly were one of a kind. Rest easy, Mick.'
stories.why_it_matters: It's a reminder that F1's spectacle rests on hundreds of largely anonymous crew members, and the sport's tight-knit paddock culture treats the loss of any one of them as a shared loss across competing teams.
stories.ripple_effects: Expect continued tributes across the grid at upcoming races; stories like this often prompt broader recognition of pit-crew and support-staff contributions in motorsport media.
stories.why_now: The team's announcement came this week, with the tribute visible during the Hungarian Grand Prix weekend.
stories.watch_next: Any further tributes or dedications planned at F1's next race after the summer break.
stories.the_lesson: Institutions — sports teams especially — are built on long-serving people whose work is invisible to outsiders but foundational to everything visible on race day.

stories.title: McLaren runs Norris, Piastri and F2 champion Fornaroli through a 2-day Portimao test
key_points: McLaren completed a **2-day private test** at Portimao, Portugal before F1's summer break.
Lando Norris drove **49 laps**, Oscar Piastri **55 laps**, and F2 champion **Leonardo Fornaroli 47 laps**.
The car used was a **2023-spec McLaren** (a 'Testing of Previous Cars' run, the only kind of in-season testing F1 rules allow).
Portimao is set to **return to the F1 calendar in 2027**, making this valuable track-learning time.
Fornaroli got to watch both race drivers' technique and feedback style up close.
stories.background: F1 severely restricts in-season testing to control costs and keep competition fair — teams can't just test their current car whenever they want. The workaround is 'Testing of Previous Cars' (TPC), where teams run an older car (here, a 2023-spec machine) at a circuit, which is allowed because it's not directly developing the current title-fighting car. Portimao, on Portugal's Algarve coast, hosted F1 races in 2020-2021 during the pandemic-shuffled calendar and is confirmed to return in 2027 under the sport's new rules cycle — so track time now is a head start for drivers and teams.
stories.what_happened: McLaren spent two days at Portimao running Lando Norris, Oscar Piastri, and Formula 2 champion Leonardo Fornaroli in a 2023-specification car, completing 49, 55, and 47 laps respectively. Strong afternoon winds added a challenge, with changing gusts affecting car balance through the lap. The test doubled as a scouting and development opportunity for Fornaroli — McLaren's likely young-driver prospect — who got to observe both current McLaren race drivers' driving style and technical feedback firsthand, having traveled straight from Budapest after his second official F1 practice outing. It came just before teams enter F1's mandated summer shutdown period.
stories.why_it_matters: With Portimao returning to the F1 calendar in 2027, early track knowledge is a real, if small, competitive edge — and the test is a visible marker of how seriously McLaren is grooming Fornaroli as a future driver.
stories.ripple_effects: Other teams (Aston Martin, Audi, Alpine) used the same testing window for their own tyre and car development at Hungary's circuit, underlining how competitive this pre-summer-break testing period has become across the grid.
stories.why_now: Teams are using the final days before F1's mandatory summer shutdown to squeeze in every permitted testing opportunity.
stories.watch_next: Whether Fornaroli gets further McLaren practice-session outings once the season resumes.

key_terms.definition: F1's rule allowing teams to run an older-spec car for testing, since testing the current car mid-season is banned to control costs.

stories.the_lesson: In heavily regulated sports, teams find creative, rules-compliant ways (like testing an old car) to keep gaining an edge even when the obvious path is blocked.

stories.title: Honda explains the mysterious engine 'oscillations' that alarmed Alonso in Hungary — and says it's fixed
key_points: Alonso reported strange **oscillations** in seventh gear on Hungary's main straight in first practice.
Honda says the cause was an **engine combustion characteristic** tied to engine temperature, not a repeat of earlier vibration problems.
Honda made **corrective adjustments** between practice sessions and says the issue was resolved.
This is a **different fault** from the vibration issue that plagued the Aston Martin-Honda power unit earlier in 2026.
Honda's next-generation engine upgrade is due to debut at the **Dutch Grand Prix**.
stories.background: Aston Martin switched to **Honda** engines for the 2026 season as part of its wider technical rebuild alongside hiring Adrian Newey, but the partnership has been dogged by reliability scares, including an earlier vibration problem severe enough that Alonso said he lost feeling in his limbs. **Trackside general manager Shintaro Orihara** leads Honda's on-the-ground engineering response to issues like these during race weekends.
stories.what_happened: During **first practice** at the Hungarian Grand Prix, Fernando Alonso radioed in about unusual **oscillations** in his Aston Martin's engine at high speed in seventh gear. Honda's engineers investigated and identified the cause as an **engine combustion characteristic** linked to how engine temperature behaved in the car's new chassis — a distinct issue from the vibration problems the team faced earlier in the season. Honda's Shintaro Orihara confirmed the team adjusted engine parameters between first and second practice and made 'good progress' resolving it. Honda says it is confident these **corrective measures** have dispelled Alonso's complaints.
stories.why_it_matters: Reliability issues like this directly threaten Alonso and Aston Martin's ability to even finish races, on top of the team's existing performance struggles — so ruling out a serious mechanical fault matters as much as any upgrade.
stories.ripple_effects: A resolved, well-understood issue reduces the risk of a race-ending failure and gives Honda more confidence heading into upcoming engine upgrades, including the one due at the Dutch Grand Prix, while a recurring or misdiagnosed issue could have forced a costly redesign.
stories.why_now: The oscillations appeared for the first time when Aston Martin ran its new-look car with a fresh chassis in Hungary, prompting an investigation that Honda concluded this week.
stories.watch_next: Watch whether the oscillation issue stays resolved once Honda's next engine upgrade debuts at the Dutch Grand Prix.

key_terms.definition: F1's term for the full hybrid engine system — the combustion engine plus its electric motors and battery — supplied by manufacturers like Honda.

stories.the_lesson: In high-performance engineering, a scary symptom like unexplained vibrations doesn't always mean a scary cause — diagnosing the actual mechanism is what separates a quick fix from a season-derailing problem.

stories.title: Adrian Newey says he's 'confident' Fernando Alonso stays at Aston Martin, as Alpine circles for 2027
key_points: Alonso is contracted at Aston Martin only through the **end of this season**, with no deal yet for 2027.
Newey says he's **'pretty confident'** Alonso will stay, calling him 'an amazing driver.'
Alonso's long-time manager **Flavio Briatore**, now an Alpine executive advisor, is pushing hard to bring him back for a fourth stint.
Alonso is reportedly waiting until **after the summer break** to decide, hoping Aston Martin's upgrades show real progress.
Aston Martin has scored just **one point** from the season's first 11 races.
stories.background: Fernando Alonso is a two-time world champion who joined **Aston Martin** in 2023 partly on the promise that design legend **Adrian Newey** — hired as the team's managing technical partner in 2025 — would eventually build him a genuinely competitive car. So far in 2026, that hasn't happened: Aston Martin has struggled at the back of the grid. Alonso has history with **Alpine** (formerly Renault), where he won both his championships in 2005-06 under team boss **Flavio Briatore**, who now holds an advisory role at Alpine and is reportedly keen to reunite with his old driver for what would be Alonso's farewell season.
stories.what_happened: Speaking in Hungary, **Adrian Newey** addressed what Alonso's potential departure would mean for Aston Martin, saying Alonso 'brings huge amounts to the team, both in his feedback and his ability,' and that he is 'pretty confident' the relationship will continue. This comes as rumours grow that Alonso could make a surprise return to **Alpine** for 2027, with Briatore and Alpine's incoming title sponsor reportedly pushing hard to sign him. Alonso himself has not decided, and is believed to be waiting until after the summer break to see whether Aston Martin's upgrades — including a near-complete new chassis — lift the team's form. Briatore, asked directly about an Alpine reunion, didn't rule it out but said Alonso remains 'an Aston Martin driver' through the end of the season.
stories.why_it_matters: Where a two-time champion central to Aston Martin's multi-year rebuild — built around Newey and a new Honda engine deal — decides to race in 2027 will shape both teams' driver markets and could signal whether Aston Martin's investment is paying off.
stories.ripple_effects: If Alonso leaves, Aston Martin would need a replacement while trying to prove its Newey-led rebuild works, and Alpine would gain a proven title-winner for its own 2027 push. It also affects the broader driver market, since other seats and contract talks — at Red Bull, Ferrari, and Williams among others — are being negotiated around the same time.
stories.why_now: This is surfacing now because Aston Martin has just brought its biggest upgrade package of the season to the Hungarian Grand Prix, giving Alonso fresh data to judge whether the team's turnaround is real before his post-summer-break decision.
stories.watch_next: Watch for Alonso's decision after the summer break, expected once Aston Martin's new-chassis performance at races like Monza and Baku becomes clear.
stories.the_lesson: In F1, driver contract decisions are rarely about loyalty alone — they hinge on concrete, near-term evidence, like a car upgrade actually working, rather than promises about a team's long-term project.
